palette: weathered teak and ochre against slate paving
topic: an empty patio photographed in september
angle: Outdoor space shot bare in September tells a buyer the garden is finished for the year. Staged, it stays a room they count. One photograph, furnished once, with the paving, the borders and the flat overcast light untouched.
visualSummary: Deep blue field carrying two numbered horizontal bands rather than three. Band one holds the bare source photograph: grey slate paving running away from the camera between two planted borders, a dark timber gate at the far end, the white rendered flank of a bungalow with a wall lantern on the right, flat overcast daylight and no furniture anywhere. Band two holds the same photograph staged farmhouse with lounge seating rather than a dining set: a weathered teak sofa on the left, two matching armchairs facing it, a low teak table between them, ochre and rust cushions, a rust fringed throw over the sofa arm and an ochre diamond patterned rug on the slate. Every seat sits on a solid slatted plinth that meets the ground rather than on legs. The gate, the borders, the wall lantern, the paving joints and the sky are identical in both bands. Weathered teak and ochre against slate grey and the blue chrome.

copy.headline: Don't shoot the patio bare.
copy.caption:
An empty patio in September just looks like dead space. Buyers count rooms. Nobody counts a slab of wet paving.

One photograph, uploaded once. Nothing in the frame moved. The furniture is new.

Try it on the patio photo you already have.

Virtually staged with Stagify.ai

quality.authorNote: Discarded. Round one furnished the patio as a six seat dining set. Rule 4 was applied and the render was opened; the automated scores understated the problem rather than overstating it. See the review block: the foreground chair had no seat and no front legs.

Kept. Same pinned source photograph. The prompt asked for lounge seating on solid slatted plinths instead of a dining set, which removes the thin members the known chair-leg artifact attaches to: the delivered frame has no furniture legs at all. Inspected at full size and cropped to both seating bases: the sofa and the near armchair are continuous slatted boxes meeting the paving with soft contact shadows, and no paving is visible through any seat. The prompt also forbade new planting, so the borders match the source and the post's own claim is true as written.

round1Blocking: Band 2 foreground centre chair had no seat panel and no front legs: a back, an apron rail and two rear legs, with open paving and a slab joint visible straight through the middle of it, at the optical centre of the frame.

Band 2 caption claimed 'Same paving, same planting, same light. The furniture is the only change' while the render had added a large planted terracotta pot and a grass clump that are not in the source photograph, making the claim false.
review.howFixed: Both were fixed at the source rather than papered over. The first was not argued with: the reviewer's description was checked against the pixels by cropping that chair out of the full resolution master and enlarging it, and it was exactly right. Rather than reroll the same dining set, the composition changed to lounge seating on solid slatted plinths, which deletes the artifact's habitat: the delivered render has no furniture legs at all. The second was fixed by forbidding new planting in the restage prompt, so the borders now match the source, and by tightening the line to 'Same paving, same borders, same grey light. Only the furnishings are new', which is true of the rug and cushions as well as the seating. The caption's unchanged list was corrected the same way.
round1Nits: A hair-width dark filament at the base of the left armchair, reading as a stray thread.
A slight outward kink in one leg above the foot where it crossed the bed edge.
nits: A small potted herb sits on the low table as styling. It is a furnishing on the furniture rather than a change to the borders, which is why the copy says furnishings rather than furniture only.
review.dashAudit: Zero dash-like glyphs in the rendered type across the whole frame. The reviewer enumerated every text element (headline, eyebrow, both step titles, both step notes, the wordmark, the footer disclosure, the CTA pill and the two numerals) and found no mark rendering as a horizontal stroke at mid height, so there was nothing to measure against a lowercase n. The only long horizontal strokes in the image are photographic: paving joints, the seat slats and the window head.
review.layoutVerdict: Reworked after the operator flagged the spacing. The template distributes band height by flex, so two bands each came out about twice as tall as the copy inside them: the numbered disc sat marooned in a top corner, the title and note floated in the middle of the card, and the card edges were too faint to say where the container was. process-strip now has a sparse mode for two bands or fewer (steps--sparse) rather than the dense scale stretched: the number stacks above the title inside the copy column, the type steps up to 42px and 28px, the card ground and border are lifted so the container reads, the photo takes 41 percent of the band and the gutter between cards opens to 24px. The band grid is otherwise unchanged, and the post still ships two bands rather than an invented third.
review.samenessVerdict: Not a rerun, but a recombination. The idea is genuinely new to the run: the first exterior, the first seasonal hook and the first empty to furnished pair shot outdoors. The composition is closest to 2026-08-16, which uses the same deep blue ground and the same two stacked rounded cards, and the numbered blue discs come from 2026-08-19. Colour is the least differentiated axis: this makes five of the last six posts on the same deep blue ground, with only 2026-08-20 on the pale wash. Worth spending the pale wash or a photo ground on the next post.
review.imageScaleFix: Both frames were recropped to the same relative window and repinned to 4:5. The masters framed a long side passage with the seating in the middle distance under roughly a third of a frame of empty foreground paving, which read as undersized furniture. The crop is identical in both frames, so the pair is still one photograph and the caption claim holds.
review.voicePass: On-image copy rewritten after the operator flagged it as reading AI-generated, checked against the 18 shipped headlines in history rather than taste. Three tells. The headline used the "X kills Y" hook formula and was the only metaphor headline on the account, where every other one states a plain fact or gives a plain instruction. Step one used "reads as", a critics verb for a voice whose own config asks for short declaratives. Step two ran an anaphoric tricolon, "Same paving, same borders, same grey light", closed by an "Only X are new" reversal, which is the most machine sounding line in the frame and a rhythm no other post on the account uses. The headline is now an instruction rather than a claim, in the shape of 2026-08-20, and step one uses "dead space", which is the trade term agents use themselves. Operator picked both from four options each. Titles are 22 characters, so both bands hold one line and the two copy blocks match, which also retires the wrap nit from the layout pass. Caption given the same pass: "reads as" replaced with the "dead space" line the frame now uses, the "What is new is the furnishings" cleft straightened to "The furniture is new", the "first thing in a listing gallery to date" pun dropped because it reads as a typo, the "the photo argues that ... at exactly the point in autumn when" clause broken into two short declaratives, and the "because the point is the furniture" reveal replaced with plain sentences. Hook still lands in the first 110 characters, inside the 125 Instagram truncates at. checkCopy passes and no banned voice phrase is present. Caption then cut from 823 characters to 272 on the operator call, dropping the furniture list, the room type and style line, and the September timing argument. The list is not lost: band two of the frame still reads "Nothing else changed. A sofa, two chairs, a table and a rug", so the claim stays checkable against the image even though the caption no longer spells it out.

devilsAdvocate.authorNote: The advocate killed this candidate (i05) and picked i01, the bedroom style grid. The operator overrode that and chose i05. The advocate's kill had two parts and both were addressed rather than ignored. It argued that the three bands held only two real states, and that band three, the same patio under warmer evening light, would be an Exterior Studio time-of-day change rather than the core-staging the candidate declared. Both are correct. The post therefore ships with two bands, which is what process-strip's own meta.rules asks for: use the real number of steps rather than padding to look slicker. Dropping band three removes the false feature claim entirely, and the caption states plainly that no sky and no time of day were changed.
